title: Max Points on a Line
description: Brute force to optimized: cross-product triple-checking versus anchor-and-slope grouping, then a fraction-based fix for a real floating point correctness bug.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a list of points on a 2D plane, find the largest number of points that all lie on a single straight line at the same time.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a list of points on a 2D plane, find the largest number of points that all lie on a single straight line at the same time.

blocks.title: Analogy: Sliding a Ruler Across a Page of Dots
blocks.text: Picture a page covered in scattered dots, and a ruler that can be placed anywhere and rotated to any angle. The goal is to find the one placement of the ruler that touches the most dots at once. Rather than trying every possible angle by hand, a smarter approach is to anchor the ruler on one dot at a time and check, for every other dot, exactly which direction it sits in, dots sharing the same direction from the anchor automatically line up together.

blocks.caption: Anchor on one point, group the rest by the direction they sit in

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: points = [1,1], [2,2], [3,3]

blocks.text: All 3 points are collinear, so the answer is 3.

Example: a single point, or exactly two points
Any 1 or 2 points are trivially considered to lie on a common line, since a line can always be drawn through 1 or 2 points, so the answer is simply the number of points given.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what "collinear" really depends on.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Three points are collinear exactly when the direction from the first to the second matches the direction from the first to the third, no rotation or measurement needed, just a direction comparison.

Observation 2: If one point is fixed as an anchor, every other point has some direction relative to it, and any two points sharing that exact same direction from the anchor automatically lie on the same line through the anchor.

Observation 3: This means the whole problem, for one anchor, reduces to grouping every other point by its direction from that anchor and finding the largest group, repeated once per possible anchor.

Observation 4: Representing direction as a floating point slope seems natural, but floating point division can round two mathematically identical directions into two slightly different numbers, so representing direction as a reduced whole number ratio instead avoids that risk entirely.
That reasoning alone already sketches the whole approach: anchor, group by direction, and be careful how "direction" is represented.
6. Brute Force Solution

The most direct approach is to check every possible pair of points, and for each pair, test every other point to see whether it also lies on the same line, using the cross product to test collinearity without ever dividing.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every pair of points i and j.
Start a count at 2, for the pair itself.
For every other point k, check whether the cross product formed by i, j, and k is zero, which means all three are collinear.
If so, increase the count.
Track the largest count seen across every pair.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every third point against every pair using the cross product

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The cross product formula tests collinearity using only multiplication and subtraction, with no division and therefore no floating point risk at all in this brute force version.
count starts at 2 for every pair, since the pair itself, i and j, always trivially counts as 2 points on whatever line is being considered.
The n <= 2 special case is handled before the main loops begin, since any 1 or 2 points are trivially collinear and the triple-nested loop logic below assumes at least 3 points exist to compare.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because the cross product of two direction vectors is exactly zero when the three points involved are collinear, a reliable test that never requires dividing by anything.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), checking every pair of points, and for each pair, every other point.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: re-testing every pair from scratch against every other point repeats a huge amount of work. A cleaner approach is to fix one point at a time and look at the direction from it to every other point, points sharing the exact same direction from that anchor are automatically collinear with it, and can all be grouped together in one pass instead of tested pair by pair.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every pair against every third point works but is wasteful: the same underlying question, whether point k lines up with the direction between some anchor and point k, keeps getting re-derived from scratch for every different pair.

What stays fixed if one point is chosen as an anchor: the anchor's own position, letting every other point's relationship to it be described by a single direction, computed once per point rather than once per pair.

Can points be grouped by that direction instead of compared pair by pair: yes, points sharing the exact same direction from the anchor are automatically all collinear with each other and with the anchor.

What is the largest line through this anchor: the size of the largest such direction group, plus the anchor itself.

The core idea: for each point as an anchor, group every other point by its direction, its slope, from that anchor, and track the largest group.

For each point used as an anchor, compute the slope from that anchor to every other point, and group points by matching slope using a hash map. The largest group found, plus the anchor point itself, gives the most points collinear through that anchor. Repeat for every possible anchor and keep the largest result.
9. Optimized Solution

Fix each point in turn as the anchor. For every other point, compute the change in x and y, and derive a slope (using a floating point division, treating a vertical line as infinity). Group points by that slope value, and track the largest group size for this anchor.
Dry run for points = [1,1], [2,2], [3,3], anchored at (1,1)

blocks.text: Both other points share the slope 1.0, so the group size is 2, plus the anchor itself gives 3.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: group every other point by its floating point slope from the anchor

codes.python:
def max_points(points):
    n = len(points)
    if n <= 2:
        return n
    max_count = 1
    for i in range(n):
        slopes = {}                      # maps a slope value to how many points share it
        duplicates = 0
        local_max = 0
        for j in range(n):
            if i == j:
                continue
            dx = points[j][0] - points[i][0]
            dy = points[j][1] - points[i][1]
            if dx == 0 and dy == 0:
                duplicates += 1            # the exact same point appears twice
                continue
            slope = float('inf') if dx == 0 else dy / dx   # floating point division, precision risk
            slopes[slope] = slopes.get(slope, 0) + 1
            local_max = max(local_max, slopes[slope])
        max_count = max(max_count, local_max + duplicates + 1)
    return max_count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    points = [[1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]]
    print(max_points(points))

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because collinearity with a fixed anchor point is entirely determined by direction: two other points lie on the same line through the anchor exactly when the direction from the anchor to each of them is identical. Grouping every other point by that computed slope, and tracking the size of the largest group, directly counts the most points collinear through that specific anchor; repeating this once per anchor and keeping the overall largest result guarantees the true best line is found, since the best line must pass through at least one of the given points, which becomes the anchor for that check.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["Two other points share the exact same slope from the anchor","They fall into the same group in the slope map","Both count toward the same potential line through the anchor"],["A point coincides exactly with the anchor, a duplicate coordinate","It is tracked separately as a duplicate, not given a slope at all","It is added to every group's final count, since a duplicate point lies on every line through that location"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Duplicate points, where dx and dy are both 0, are tracked in a separate duplicates counter rather than being given a slope, since a point at the exact same location as the anchor cannot meaningfully be assigned a direction, yet it does belong on every line through the anchor.

A vertical line, where dx is 0 and dy is nonzero, is assigned the special slope value infinity specifically to avoid a division by zero, while still giving every point sharing that same vertical line an identical, matching key.
local_max plus duplicates plus 1, for the anchor itself, is computed once per anchor, and the running maxCount only updates if this anchor's best line beats every anchor checked so far.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), a genuine complexity class improvement, one pass over every other point for each anchor.
Space: O(n), for the slope map at each anchor.
10. Further Optimization: Fraction Based Slopes, No Floating Point

Using a floating point division to represent a slope is a well known source of bugs in this exact problem. Two directions that are mathematically identical, like 1 divided by 3 and 2 divided by 6, can come out as slightly different floating point values due to rounding, causing them to be incorrectly placed in different groups and producing a wrong answer.

The fix: instead of dividing at all, reduce dx and dy to their simplest whole number ratio using their greatest common divisor, and use that exact pair of whole numbers as the grouping key. Two directions that are truly the same will always reduce to the exact same pair, with no rounding involved anywhere.
Dry run for points = [1,1], [2,2], [3,3], anchored at (1,1)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Other point","dx, dy","gcd","Reduced key","Why"],"rows":[["(2,2)","1, 1","1","(1, 1)","dx and dy are already in their simplest form, since their gcd is 1."],["(3,3)","2, 2","2","(1, 1)","Dividing both 2 and 2 by their gcd, 2, reduces this direction down to exactly the same key as the point above."]]}

blocks.text: Both directions reduce to the exact same key, (1, 1), grouped correctly with no floating point involved at any point, giving the same correct answer of 3.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: reduce each direction to a whole number ratio, eliminating floating point entirely

codes.python:
from math import gcd

def max_points(points):
    n = len(points)
    if n <= 2:
        return n
    max_count = 1
    for i in range(n):
        slopes = {}                      # maps a reduced (dx, dy) direction to how many points share it
        duplicates = 0
        local_max = 0
        for j in range(n):
            if i == j:
                continue
            dx = points[j][0] - points[i][0]
            dy = points[j][1] - points[i][1]
            if dx == 0 and dy == 0:
                duplicates += 1
                continue
            g = gcd(dx, dy)              # reduce the direction to its simplest whole number form
            dx, dy = dx // g, dy // g
            if dx < 0:
                dx, dy = -dx, -dy          # normalize sign so opposite directions share one key
            key = (dx, dy)
            slopes[key] = slopes.get(key, 0) + 1
            local_max = max(local_max, slopes[key])
        max_count = max(max_count, local_max + duplicates + 1)
    return max_count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    points = [[1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]]
    print(max_points(points))

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The greatest common divisor of dx and dy is computed using their absolute values, since gcd is only meaningfully defined for non-negative numbers, even though dx or dy individually may be negative.

Dividing both dx and dy by their gcd reduces the direction to its simplest whole number form, so any two directions that are truly identical, no matter how large the original coordinates were, always reduce to the exact same pair.

Normalizing the sign, forcing dx to be non-negative and flipping dy's sign to match if needed, ensures that two exactly opposite directions, like (1,2) and (-1,-2), which represent the same line, are always mapped to the same key rather than being treated as different groups.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same order as the floating point version.
Space: O(n). This round is not about speed, it is a genuine correctness fix, eliminating a real source of wrong answers on inputs where floating point precision would otherwise fail.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is fixing an anchor point and grouping everything else by direction relative to it, turning an O(n cubed) all-pairs-and-a-third-point check into an O(n squared) grouping problem. Equally important is the lesson that floating point comparisons are unreliable for exact equality checks, and reducing to a whole number fraction is the standard, safe fix whenever exact directions need to be compared.
Common Mistakes

items: Comparing floating point slopes directly for equality, which can silently produce wrong answers on certain inputs due to rounding.
Forgetting to handle duplicate points, the exact same coordinates appearing more than once, which are collinear with every line through that location.
Forgetting to normalize the sign of the reduced direction, without it, opposite directions like (1, 2) and (-1, -2) would be treated as different lines when they are actually the same.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is one of the clearest real world demonstrations of why floating point should be avoided for exact comparisons. Proactively mentioning the floating point precision risk, and proposing the gcd based fraction fix without being asked, signals strong attention to correctness, not just getting a solution that passes the obvious test cases.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every triple", think: anchor on one point at a time and group the rest by direction.
If the interviewer says "is floating point safe here", think: no, reduce dx and dy to a whole number ratio using their gcd instead.
If the interviewer says "what about duplicate points", think: track them separately and add them to every group's count, since they never define their own direction.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Can you construct a concrete input where the floating point slope version would give a wrong answer?
Why must the sign of the reduced (dx, dy) pair be normalized?
How would you handle duplicate points if the problem asked for the maximum line through distinct points only?
Can you extend this anchor-and-group technique to count collinear points in 3D space?
What is the overall time complexity if there are many duplicate points among the input?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "compare directions or slopes for exact equality" problem, which should generally avoid floating point and prefer reduced integer ratios instead, the same fix applied here.

Anchor-and-group techniques in general, fixing one element and grouping the rest by some derived relationship, which reappears in problems beyond geometry, like grouping strings by a canonical signature.
Convex hull and other computational geometry problems, which share this problem's broader theme of reasoning about points, directions, and collinearity.
GCD based normalization, which shows up whenever two ratios need to be compared for exact mathematical equality without rounding error, such as simplifying fractions in general.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force triple-checking approach runs in O(n cubed) time and O(1) space. The slope grouping approach, whether using floating point or reduced fractions, runs in O(n squared) time and O(n) space, a genuine complexity class improvement. The fraction based version is not faster than the floating point version, it exists to fix a real correctness bug that floating point precision can otherwise introduce.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: fixing an anchor point and grouping every other point by direction relative to it, using reduced integer fractions instead of floating point slopes to avoid a real precision bug.

Core Idea: two points share a line through a fixed anchor exactly when their direction from that anchor matches; grouping by direction, using a gcd-reduced, sign-normalized (dx, dy) pair as the key instead of a floating point slope, finds the largest such group correctly and without rounding risk.
Time: O(n cubed) for the brute force, O(n squared) for both the floating point and fraction based grouping versions.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for both grouping versions.

Most Important Observation: this problem's final optimization round is not about speed, both slope based versions run at the same O(n squared), it is a genuine correctness fix, since floating point equality is fundamentally unreliable for this exact use case.

Interview Difficulty: the anchor-and-group idea itself is a moderate leap from the brute force, but proactively catching and fixing the floating point precision risk is what distinguishes a truly strong answer.
One line memory trick: anchor on a point, group the rest by a gcd-reduced direction, never compare floating point slopes for exact equality.
